section.title: Cast Your Burden on the Lord
section.sectionRationale: A Maskil of David marked by an especially painful betrayal, not from an enemy but from a man like myself, my companion and close friend, verses 12-14. The psalm moves from anguished longing to flee, through the shock of intimate betrayal, to the settled confidence that closes the psalm and is later quoted almost word for word in 1 Peter 5:7.
section.thesis: Betrayed by a close friend and companion, not merely an enemy, David pours out his anguish and longs to flee, yet resolves to cast his burden on the LORD, who sustains the righteous, a pattern that anticipates Jesus, betrayed by His own familiar friend.
section.frameNote: Three movements: David's anguish and longing to flee like a dove; the shock of betrayal by a close companion amid a city full of violence; and the closing resolve to cast every burden on the LORD, who will never let the righteous be shaken.

units.label: Oh, that I had wings like a dove
units.note: anguish and the longing to flee

verses.text: Listen to my prayer, O God, and do not ignore my plea.
Attend to me and answer me. I am restless in my complaint, and distraught
at the voice of the enemy, at the pressure of the wicked. For they release disaster upon me and revile me in their anger.
My heart murmurs within me, and the terrors of death assail me.
Fear and trembling grip me, and horror has overwhelmed me.
I said, “Oh, that I had wings like a {{yonah|dove}}! I would fly away and find rest.
How far away I would flee! In the wilderness I would remain. Selah
I would hurry to my shelter, far from this raging tempest.”

units.label: It is you, my companion and close friend

verses.text: O Lord, confuse and confound their speech, for I see violence and strife in the city.
Day and night they encircle the walls, while malice and trouble lie within.
Destruction is within; oppression and deceit never leave the streets.
For it is not an enemy who insults me; that I could endure. It is not a foe who rises against me; from him I could hide.
But it is you, a man like myself, my companion and close friend.
We shared sweet {{sod|fellowship}} together; we walked with the crowd into the house of God.

Let death seize them by surprise; let them go down to Sheol alive, 
for evil is with them in their homes.

units.label: Cast your burden upon the Lord

verses.text: But I call to God, and the LORD saves me.
Morning, noon, and night, I cry out in distress, and He hears my voice.

He redeems my soul in peace from the battle waged against me, 
even though many oppose me.
God will hear and humiliate them, the One enthroned for the ages, Selah because they do not change and they have no fear of God.
My companion attacks his friends; he violates his covenant.
His speech is smooth as butter, but war is in his heart. His words are softer than oil, yet they are swords unsheathed.

{{shalak|Cast}} your burden upon the LORD and He will sustain you; 
He will never let the righteous be shaken.

But You, O God, will bring them down to the Pit of destruction; men of bloodshed and deceit will not live out half their days. 
But I will trust in You.

yonah.gloss: Dove. David longs for a dove's wings to escape entirely, a natural human longing to flee overwhelming pain rather than face it, a longing Scripture takes seriously even as it leads David, by the psalm's end, to trust rather than flight.

sod.gloss: Close, intimate fellowship or shared counsel. David and his betrayer once had sod together, deep, trusted companionship, which makes the betrayal in verses 12-14 all the more devastating; this was no stranger but a confidant.

shalak.gloss: To cast, to throw. David's command to himself, cast your burden upon the LORD, pictures a deliberate, decisive action of transferring a weight he cannot carry onto the one who can, language 1 Peter 5:7 echoes almost word for word.

basic.context: This psalm captures a uniquely painful kind of suffering: betrayal not by an enemy but by a close friend, someone with whom David once shared sweet fellowship and walked into God's house side by side. David first longs simply to escape entirely, wishing for a dove's wings to fly away from it all. But the psalm does not end there; it moves through the shock of betrayal to a settled resolve to cast every burden on the LORD, who sustains the righteous.
basic.hermeneutics: The psalm gives full voice to real anguish, including the natural, human longing to flee overwhelming pain, without treating that longing as sinful in itself. Its resolution comes not by escaping the situation but by transferring the weight of it to God, a pattern of prayer meant to be imitated whenever betrayal or overwhelming pressure strikes.
basic.originalLanguages: David longs for the wings of a yonah, a dove, to fly away entirely. His grief is sharpened because he once shared sod, intimate fellowship, with his betrayer. The psalm's turning point comes in the command shalak, cast, your burden upon the LORD, decisively transferring what cannot be carried alone.
basic.typology: The betrayal by a close companion who shared table fellowship, described in verses 12-14, anticipates the betrayal of Jesus by Judas, one of His own twelve disciples, a companion entrusted with intimate fellowship who nonetheless turned against Him.
basic.christ: Verses 12-14 describe betrayal by a man like myself, my companion and close friend, one who shared sweet fellowship and walked with David into God's house. This directly anticipates Judas' betrayal of Jesus, one of His own twelve disciples who shared table fellowship with Him, John 13:18, quoting the closely related Psalm 41:9. Just as David entrusted himself to God rather than taking vengeance, Jesus, betrayed by His own familiar friend, entrusted Himself to the Father who judges justly, 1 Peter 2:23, and the psalm's closing counsel, cast your burden on the LORD, is applied directly to every believer, 1 Peter 5:7.
basic.god: God is shown as the one who hears the cry of the betrayed at every hour, morning, noon, and night, and who sustains the righteous even amid ongoing treachery, never allowing them to be finally shaken, while remaining the enthroned Judge who will hold the treacherous to account.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Peter 5:7 quotes this psalm's counsel almost word for word, casting all your anxiety on Him because He cares for you. John 13:18 shows Jesus applying kindred betrayal-by-a-friend language to Judas. Matthew 26:36-39 shows Jesus in Gethsemane entrusting Himself fully to the Father amid the anguish of imminent betrayal and death.
basic.oneStory: Betrayed by an intimate friend, David longs to flee, but instead learns to cast his burden on the LORD, who sustains the righteous. That same pattern of betrayal met by trust reaches its height in Jesus, betrayed by His own familiar friend, who entrusted Himself to the Father and now invites every burdened believer to cast their anxiety on Him.

context.literary:
Psalm 55 does not move in a straight line, and that is part of its craft. A tidy lament goes from complaint to trust in one direction. This one circles. It complains, verses 1 to 8, prays against the city, verses 9 to 11, breaks into the betrayal, verses 12 to 15, declares trust, verses 16 to 19, and then goes back to the betrayer, verses 20 and 21, before it finishes with counsel and a vow, verses 22 and 23. The mind of a wounded man keeps returning to the wound. The psalm lets the reader feel it.

The pronouns tell the same story. In verses 12 to 14 the betrayer is addressed directly, 'it is you,' and the sentence breaks off in a cry. In verses 20 and 21 he is spoken of at a distance, 'My companion attacks his friends.' Then verse 22 shifts again to a command in the second person, 'Cast your burden upon the LORD,' spoken to a hearer who may be the singer's own soul or the congregation. The last verse ends with a defiant 'But I will trust in You,' set against the men of bloodshed and deceit.

The psalm is also built around time. Violence walks the walls 'day and night' in verse 10, and the psalmist answers with prayer at 'morning, noon, and night' in verse 17. The enemy keeps a watch, and so does the man who prays. The city imagery is worth noticing too: walls and streets appear in verses 9 to 11. Malice and trouble are pictured as guards on the wall, while ruin, oppression and deceit sit in the streets. The city is not under siege from outside; it is rotten within.

Finally, the psalm is bracketed by two verses that use the word 'I' against a crowd. Verse 1 is the singer's cry, and verse 23 is the singer's resolve. Between them the cry is transformed, not silenced.
context.historical:
The heading names David and calls the psalm a Maskil, but it gives no occasion. The details still fit one crisis in his life well: the revolt of his son Absalom. The city with violence and strife in its streets, verses 9 to 11, is Jerusalem at the time of the uprising. David's own words at the start of the crisis were 'Arise and let us flee,' 2 Samuel 15:14, and the wish to fly to the wilderness in verse 7 matches the way he actually left: 'the king crossed the Kidron Valley, and all the people also passed toward the way of the wilderness,' 2 Samuel 15:23.

The betrayer of the psalm fits Ahithophel, whom Absalom summoned during the sacrifices that were part of the revolt, 2 Samuel 15:12. He was David's own counsellor, and his advice was regarded 'like the consultation of the word of God,' 2 Samuel 16:23. When David heard that Ahithophel was among the conspirators, he prayed a short prayer, 'O LORD, please turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness,' 2 Samuel 15:31, which is close in spirit to the request of verse 9 of the psalm. Ahithophel later hanged himself when his counsel was ignored, 2 Samuel 17:23, which resembles the verdict of verse 23 that bloodthirsty and deceitful men will not live out half their days. Tradition has long read these verses that way. The psalm never names him, and the fit is an inference, not a statement.

The friendship the psalm looks back on was a religious one. 'We walked with the crowd into the house of God' describes pilgrim processions to the sanctuary, a picture of two men joined in public worship. To the first hearers this made the treachery a betrayal of a shared faith as well as of a friendship. The word 'covenant' in verse 20 belongs to that world, where friendships between leaders could be sealed by oath, as David and Jonathan's was, 1 Samuel 18:3.

The dove of verse 6 was a common bird of the Judean cliffs and clefts. The wilderness the singer longs for was, for David, no daydream but the actual place he was headed.
context.canonical:
Psalm 55 is the longest of a run of psalms of David in distress, and it has one of the most quoted lines in the Psalter. Its counsel, 'Cast your burden upon the LORD and He will sustain you,' verse 22, is echoed in the New Testament: 'Cast all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you,' 1 Peter 5:7. Peter does not introduce the line as a quotation, so it is best called an echo, but the shape is the same and the Greek word for the burden in the Septuagint is the word for anxiety in Peter. The line also lies close to Psalm 68:19, 'Blessed be the Lord, who daily bears our burden,' and to Psalm 37:5, 'Commit your way to the LORD.'

The betrayal by an intimate is a Psalter theme. Psalm 41:9 speaks of the 'close friend whom I trusted, the one who shared my bread' who 'has lifted up his heel against me.' Jesus quotes that verse of Judas in John 13:18. Psalm 55 is never quoted directly in the New Testament, but it deepens the same theme and adds the note of covenant broken.

Other links widen the picture. Verse 15, 'let them go down to Sheol alive,' recalls the judgment on Korah in Numbers 16:30. The prayer that God would confuse the enemies' speech in verse 9 recalls Babel, where God confused human language, Genesis 11:7, although the psalm uses its own verbs. And the closing promise that the righteous will not be shaken lines up with the confidence of Psalm 16:8 and Psalm 62:2, both taken up in the apostles' preaching, Acts 2:25.

The final assurance about the Pit of destruction also invites a comparison with Psalm 16:10, where the Holy One is not abandoned to Sheol or allowed to see decay, a verse Peter and Paul both apply to Christ, Acts 2:27, 13:35.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The poet meant to be honest about how betrayal feels, and to show that honesty is not the enemy of faith. He does not tidy the wish to flee, the fear, or the fury. He puts them all in a prayer, and lets the prayer take him somewhere. The first hearers would have understood that pain of this kind does not resolve in one movement, and the winding shape of the psalm gives them permission to come back to the same hurt more than once.

He also meant to teach the difference between two kinds of enemy. An outright foe can be avoided, verse 12. A friend cannot, because a friend is inside the defences. The point is not that friendship is dangerous but that the deepest wounds come from those who were closest. The psalm names the covenant-breaking and the smooth speech as the marks of the betrayer, so that Israel could recognise both.

And he meant to make the imperative of verse 22 the centre of gravity. After a psalm of movement and cry, the counsel is stated simply: hand it over. The one who gives it has done so himself, verse 16, 'But I call to God.' The hearers are meant to see that the trust David commends is one he has practised in the very pit that he describes. The psalm ends not on the resolved crisis but on a decision, 'I will trust in You.'
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Most of the psalm describes: the singer's fear, his wish for wings, the betrayal, the smooth speech, and the prayer that his enemies go down to Sheol alive. These are the words of a man in extremity, offered to God, and no one is told to copy every feeling in them. The wish to flee is presented as a real wish, not a sin, but it is not the resolution either; the psalm does not end with the flight.

The command of verse 22 is different. It is written in the imperative, and the promise attached to it, that God will sustain and not let the righteous be shaken, is meant to be taken at face value. That is why Peter can draw on it for the church. Burdens are to be handed to God, not hidden and not endlessly rehearsed. The verse leaves room for grief and tears, since the psalm itself is full of both. What it removes is the assumption that the weight has to be carried alone.

The prayers against the betrayer in verses 9, 15 and 23 belong with the description, and are best read as the plea of the wronged that God judge, not as a rule to wish ruin on those who hurt us. Jesus, who loved His betrayer enough to call him 'Friend,' Matthew 26:50, is the fuller pattern.

debates.question: Who is the friend who betrayed the psalmist?

views.label: Ahithophel, David's counsellor
views.case: The events of Absalom's revolt match the psalm closely: a city in turmoil, a flight toward the wilderness, and a trusted adviser who joined the conspirators, 2 Samuel 15:12 and 31. Ahithophel's death by hanging fits the psalm's picture of a short life for the deceitful, 2 Samuel 17:23. This is the view of long tradition.

views.label: An unnamed friend, deliberately left general
views.case: The heading gives no occasion, and the psalm names no one. Some see this as intentional: because the betrayer is anonymous, the psalm can be prayed by any believer who has been betrayed, at any time. On this view the historical fit with Absalom is possible but is not what the psalm itself insists on.

views.label: A composite of Israel's experience
views.case: Others hold that the psalm, gathered into the Psalter, stands for the whole community's experience of treacherous leaders. The move from 'you' to 'he' in verses 12 and 20 is then read as a stylised way of speaking about a type.

debates.bearing: Whichever view is held, the psalm's point is the same: the betrayal is by one who shared worship and a covenant. That is what gives the psalm its force, and what makes it a natural companion to the Gospel accounts of Judas.

debates.question: What does 'they do not change' in verse 19 mean?

views.label: They do not change their ways
views.case: The line ends, 'they have no fear of God.' The two clauses read as cause and effect: because they do not fear God, they never repent. The BSB takes this line, and it fits the picture of men who go on in deceit.

views.label: They have no reversals of fortune
views.case: The Hebrew word can also mean 'changes' in the sense of shifts in circumstance. Then the complaint is that the wicked are untroubled, a theme that runs through the Psalter, as in Psalm 73:12, and that God will hear and put an end to their ease.

debates.bearing: On either reading the verse gives a reason for God to act: the wicked show no sign of stopping. That keeps the imprecation in the psalm anchored in the persistence of the wrong, not in the singer's private anger.

debates.question: Is the wish to fly away in verses 6 to 8 a lapse of faith?

views.label: A human longing that the psalm honestly records
views.case: The wish is stated inside quotation marks, 'I said,' and then set aside. Jeremiah voices the same longing, 'If only I had a traveler's lodge in the wilderness,' Jeremiah 9:2. Scripture records such wishes without condemning them.

views.label: A temptation the psalm overcomes
views.case: Others see the wish as the temptation to escape responsibility, which the psalm answers in verse 22. On this view the movement from flight to trust is the whole point.

debates.bearing: The psalm treats the desire to run as real and the decision to trust as better. It allows both to be prayed.

study.originalLanguages:
The prayer of verse 9 uses a pair of verbs that is easy to miss in English. 'Confuse and confound their speech' translates a verb meaning 'swallow up' followed by a verb meaning 'divide.' The second verb belongs to the same family as the name Peleg, 'because in his days the earth was divided,' Genesis 10:25. Whether or not the psalmist meant to hint at Babel, the prayer is that the plotters' shared language fall apart, so that their conspiracy cannot hold together. That is exactly what happened to Absalom's council when Ahithophel's advice was set aside, 2 Samuel 17:14.

The names used for the friend in verse 13 are among the most intimate in Hebrew. 'A man like myself' means someone of my own rank or measure. 'My companion' is alluf, the word for an intimate confidant. Proverbs 16:28 says that a gossip 'divides close friends,' with the same word, and Jeremiah 3:4 uses it for the 'friend from youth.' The third term, 'close friend,' comes from the root for knowing, so it describes someone known and knowing. Three terms, one after another, pile up the closeness so that the betrayal lands with full weight.

Verse 14's 'sweet fellowship' has been mentioned in the basic text with the word sod, the circle of counsel. Its reach is wider than the term suggests. Proverbs 3:32 says the LORD is 'a friend to the upright,' the same word, and Psalm 25:14 says that the LORD 'confides in those who fear Him.' A sod is a place where secrets are shared and trusted. The psalmist lost that kind of circle.

The 'redeems my soul in peace' of verse 18 uses padah, to ransom or set free. David uses the same verb of himself in 2 Samuel 4:9, 'who has redeemed my life from all distress,' and Psalm 34:22 says that 'the LORD redeems His servants.' Nothing in the word requires a price paid to a buyer. It describes a rescue that comes at God's initiative, and here it comes 'in peace,' shalom, the state of being made whole, in the middle of the battle.

Verse 22 promises that God 'will sustain' the one who casts his burden. The verb is kilkel, which means to provide for, to feed, to hold up. Joseph uses it when he says, 'I will provide for you,' Genesis 45:11 and 50:21, and it is used of Obadiah feeding a hundred prophets in caves, 1 Kings 18:4. The 'burden' itself is a rare word, and the Septuagint renders it with the Greek word for care or anxiety, the word Peter takes over in 1 Peter 5:7. The promise is that the LORD will not merely relieve but will feed and keep the one who trusts.

Finally, 'men of bloodshed and deceit' in verse 23 joins two words that Psalm 5:6 also pairs: 'the LORD abhors the man of bloodshed and deceit.' The two words describe the betrayer well, for his tongue does the work of the sword.

typology.type: The king who leaves Jerusalem by the Kidron, verses 6 to 8
typology.fulfillment: David fled the city across the Kidron Valley and went up the Mount of Olives weeping, with his head covered, 2 Samuel 15:23 and 30, when a trusted man turned against him. On the night of His betrayal, Jesus 'went out with His disciples across the Kidron Valley,' John 18:1, into a garden on the same mountain. The correspondence is deliberate in John's telling. The rejected king leaves the city in the same way by the same path, betrayed by an intimate. It also shows the escalation: David was returning to reclaim his city, while Jesus went to give His life for it. The type falls short because David left to save his own throne; Christ went out to be handed over.

typology.type: The false friend and the smooth speech, verses 12 to 14 and 20 to 21
typology.fulfillment: The psalm describes a companion whose 'words are softer than oil, yet they are swords unsheathed.' At the moment of arrest, Judas came to Jesus, said 'Greetings, Rabbi!' and kissed Him, Matthew 26:49. Jesus answered with a question that names the treachery, 'Judas, are you betraying the Son of Man with a kiss?' Luke 22:48. The kiss is the fulfilment of the smooth word with the drawn sword behind it. The escalation is that this betrayer sat at the table of the Lord Himself, John 13:26. The type falls short in that Ahithophel's betrayal was a political revolt, while Judas' was of the Messiah and led to the cross.

typology.type: Wings for a dove, and the offered rest, verses 6 to 8
typology.fulfillment: The singer longs to fly away to find rest, and then discovers that rest is found by handing the weight to God. Jesus turns that longing into an invitation: 'Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest,' Matthew 11:28. Hebrews says 'a Sabbath rest for the people of God' remains, and that whoever enters it 'rests from his own work,' Hebrews 4:9 and 10. Christ becomes the place of refuge that the dove was looking for, and the wilderness is no longer needed. The type falls short in that David's rest was a wish, while the rest of Christ is a fact for those who come.

typology.type: The righteous who will not be shaken, verse 22
typology.fulfillment: The promise that God will never let the righteous be shaken finds its fullest meaning in the one Righteous Man. Peter, quoting David on Christ, says, 'because He is at my right hand, I will not be shaken,' Acts 2:25. The resurrection is God's proof that the Righteous One was not left in the Pit, Acts 2:27. The escalation is that the assurance given to a sufferer in the psalm is secured in the One who passed through the worst and was raised. The type falls short only in the sense that the psalm's promise, for ordinary believers, still awaits its full outworking at the resurrection.

study.christ:
The psalm leads to Christ by the deepest of its themes, the friend who betrays. The New Testament does not quote Psalm 55 by name, but it quotes the sister psalm, Psalm 41:9, in John 13:18, where Jesus says, 'The one who shares My bread has lifted up his heel against Me.' Psalm 55 adds detail that the Gospels then supply. The friend sat with Him at table, 'one of the Twelve,' Mark 14:43. His words were smooth, 'Greetings, Rabbi!' Matthew 26:49. His act was a kiss that hid a sword. And Jesus called him 'Friend,' Matthew 26:50, meeting the covenant-breaker with the last word of a covenant that He would not break.

It leads to Christ by the shape of the night. David crossed the Kidron in tears, up the Mount of Olives, when Ahithophel's treachery came out, 2 Samuel 15:23 and 30. Jesus crossed the same valley, John 18:1, and in the garden the fear the psalm describes in verses 4 and 5 becomes His own: 'My soul is consumed with sorrow to the point of death,' Matthew 26:38. Mark says He was 'deeply troubled and distressed,' Mark 14:33. The terrors of death that assailed David's heart took hold of the Son, and Hebrews adds that He 'offered up prayers and petitions with loud cries and tears to the One who could save Him from death,' Hebrews 5:7. Where David asked for wings, Jesus prayed, 'My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from Me. Yet not as I will, but as You will,' Matthew 26:39. He did not fly. He cast His burden on the Father and walked to the cross.

It leads to Christ by the burden itself. Peter tells believers to cast their anxiety on Christ because He cares, 1 Peter 5:7. He can bear it because He has borne more. He 'bore our sins in His body on the tree,' 1 Peter 2:24, and He 'carried our sorrows,' Isaiah 53:4. The promise 'He will sustain you' is not that God will remove the storm but that the One who was shaken for us will not let us be.

It leads to Christ by the promise of the last verse. God 'will bring them down to the Pit of destruction' while the righteous will not be shaken. The apostles saw that promise fulfilled in Jesus, who was not abandoned to Sheol nor allowed to see decay, Acts 2:27. The betrayer went to his own end, Matthew 27:5. The Betrayed rose.

A caution: Ahithophel was not Christ, and David's prayers against his betrayers are not Jesus' prayers. What the psalm supplies is a pattern the Gospels then confirm, of the anointed man wounded by a friend and vindicated by God, together with an invitation the risen Lord makes His own.
study.god:
The psalm shows a God who hears at every hour. The singer prays 'morning, noon, and night,' verse 17, and the promise is not that God will eventually get round to him but that 'He hears my voice.' The God of the psalm does not keep office hours. Daniel prays three times a day in a later crisis, Daniel 6:10, and the pattern is the same: the answer to a watched city is a prayed-over day.

He is the God who is 'enthroned for the ages,' verse 19. The line places the whole psalm in a longer view. The betrayer and the crowd are the affairs of a season; the One who hears is the King of old, as Psalm 74:12 puts it, 'God is my King from ancient times.' His throne pre-dates every conspiracy and will outlast it. That is the ground of the confidence in verse 16, 'the LORD saves me.' The singer changes from 'God' to 'the LORD' at just the point where he needs the covenant God most.

He is a God who redeems in peace. Verse 18 says He redeems the soul from the battle 'in peace,' even while the fight goes on. The point is that inner peace is a gift of God in the middle of unresolved trouble and does not wait for the peace treaty. Jesus later says, 'Peace I leave with you; My peace I give to you,' John 14:27, and the psalm shows what that looks like in David.

He is a God who carries burdens, not one who orders us to be strong. The invitation to 'cast your burden' assumes the burden is too heavy for the person, and assumes God is strong enough for it. Psalm 68:19 calls Him the God 'who daily bears our burden.' The care is daily, personal and heavy.

He is just. The psalm asks Him to act against the men of bloodshed and deceit, and it trusts Him to do so without the singer taking a hand. He does not tolerate covenant-breaking. At the same time, the word for the righteous, 'He will never let the righteous be shaken,' is a statement about God's faithfulness to those who trust Him, since 'righteous' here describes people who take refuge in Him, not perfect people.

For worship, the psalm teaches us to be honest about fear before a God who is not frightened by it, to call on Him at all hours, and to answer the whisper 'If only I could fly away' with the deliberate sentence 'But I will trust in You.'

crossReferences.note: Absalom sends for Ahithophel the Gilonite, David's counsellor, while he is offering sacrifices. The conspiracy 'gained strength.' Many readers see here the friend of the psalm, drawn away by the revolt at the very time of worship, which echoes the 'house of God' of verse 14.

David hears that Ahithophel is among the conspirators and prays that the LORD would turn his counsel into foolishness. This is the narrative counterpart of Psalm 55:9, where the singer asks God to confuse the plotters' speech. In both, the prayer is the weapon.

When Ahithophel's advice is not followed, he goes home, puts his house in order and hangs himself. If he is the friend of the psalm, this is the short life of the man 'of bloodshed and deceit' in verse 23. The connection is an inference, not stated.

'Even my close friend whom I trusted, the one who shared my bread, has lifted up his heel against me.' The nearest kin of Psalm 55:12 to 14. Where Psalm 55 gives the pain and the covenant-breaking, Psalm 41 gives the table fellowship that John 13:18 applies to Judas.

Moses says that if the LORD opens the earth so that the rebels 'go down alive into Sheol,' the people will know they treated Him with contempt. Psalm 55:15 uses the same picture, asking that God make the judgment on treachery as plain as it was on Korah's company.

'If only I had a traveler's lodge in the wilderness, I would abandon my people and depart from them.' Jeremiah, grieved by betrayal, voices a wish much like the dove's in verse 6. The parallel shows that even the prophets wanted out, and that the wish was honestly prayed.

'Because He is at my right hand, I will not be shaken.' The same verb as the closing promise of Psalm 55:22 that God will never let the righteous be shaken. Peter takes Psalm 16 to Christ in Acts 2:25, and so gives the assurance of Psalm 55 its ultimate footing.

'Blessed be the Lord, who daily bears our burden.' A praise-response to the counsel of Psalm 55:22. The command to cast the burden and the confession that God bears it daily complete each other: one says what to do, the other says who receives it.

Judas arrives with a crowd armed with swords and clubs, greets Jesus, and kisses Him. Jesus answers, 'Friend, do what you came for.' The smooth speech and hidden sword of Psalm 55:21 have a human face here, and the Lord's reply shows the covenant love the betrayer had broken.

'He offered up prayers and petitions with loud cries and tears to the One who could save Him from death, and He was heard.' It gives the answer to the singer's cry in Psalm 55:1 to 5: the Son cried out in the same terror, and the Father heard.

'Cast all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you.' The clearest New Testament echo of Psalm 55:22. Peter adds the reason the psalm implies but does not state, that God cares, and he writes it to a church under pressure.

study.oneStory:
The psalm belongs to a story that begins with a broken friendship in a garden. In Genesis 3 the man and woman hide from God, and in Genesis 4 a brother kills a brother. From that point on the Bible has to deal with trust that turns into treachery. Psalm 55 is one of the places where the wound is felt most sharply, because the betrayer is not a stranger. What went wrong in Eden shows up in David's house: the closest are the ones who can hurt most.

Yet the psalm also answers something. In a world where trust fails, there is one to whom you can hand everything. The command to cast the burden on the LORD is the promise of a God who does not betray. The rest of the Bible confirms it. The prophets who long for a lodge in the wilderness are shown a shepherd who will gather. The people who trust in the LORD find that He sustains them through exile and return. The psalm's 'never shaken' is a line the whole Bible earns, one generation at a time.

At the centre stands Jesus, who is the fullest answer to the psalm. He is betrayed by a friend at a table, crosses the Kidron Valley, prays in fear, and is handed over with a kiss. He does not fly away. He carries the burden of sin to the cross and, in rising, shows that the righteous were never abandoned to the Pit. Then He turns to the burdened and says, 'Come to Me.' The wish for wings is answered not by an escape from the world but by a person.

The story ends where the psalm's longing points, in a city that is the opposite of the one in verses 9 to 11. Instead of violence on the walls and deceit in the streets, the Bible ends with a city where 'the throne of God and of the Lamb will be within the city,' Revelation 22:3, where there is no more curse and no more night. Betrayal is finished. The friends of God will 'see His face,' Revelation 22:4, and the burden that was cast on Him will be gone for good.

quiz.q: What does David long for in verses 6-8, and why?

options.text: The wings of a dove, to fly away entirely and escape overwhelming pressure and danger.
options.note: Verses 6-8 express this vivid, honest longing to flee rather than face the crisis.

options.text: A larger army to defeat his enemies.
options.note: David's longing here is to escape, not to gain military strength.

options.text: Wealth sufficient to bribe his enemies into peace.
options.note: This is not mentioned; the longing expressed is purely to flee to a place of rest.

options.text: A quick resolution through open confrontation with his enemies.
options.note: David expresses a desire to flee and hide, not to confront his enemies directly.

quiz.q: What makes the betrayal described in verses 12-14 especially painful for David?

options.text: It came from a close companion and friend with whom he shared fellowship, not from an enemy or stranger.
options.note: David states directly that an enemy's insult he could endure, but this betrayal came from an intimate companion.

options.text: It came from a completely unknown attacker.
options.note: The text specifies the betrayer was known intimately to David, not a stranger.

options.text: It happened publicly rather than in private.
options.note: The setting is not the main point of the pain; the intimacy of the relationship is what David highlights.

options.text: It involved the loss of significant property.
options.note: The psalm's focus is relational betrayal, not material or property loss.

quiz.q: What is the psalm's counsel in verse 22, later quoted in the New Testament?

options.text: Cast your burden upon the LORD and He will sustain you; He will never let the righteous be shaken.
options.note: 1 Peter 5:7 echoes this verse almost word for word, applying it to every believer's anxieties.

options.text: Carry your burden alone, and trust no one.
options.note: This is the opposite of the psalm's actual counsel, which is to give the burden to God, not to bear it in isolation.

options.text: Avoid prayer until the crisis has fully passed.
options.note: The psalm models constant prayer, morning, noon, and night, verse 17, not avoidance of prayer.

options.text: Seek revenge personally before trusting God.
options.note: The psalm leaves vengeance to God, verse 23, rather than commending personal revenge.

quiz.q: How does the psalm's picture of betrayal by a close friend connect to the New Testament?

options.text: It anticipates Judas' betrayal of Jesus, one of His own twelve disciples who shared table fellowship with Him.
options.note: John 13:18 draws on this same theme of betrayal by an intimate companion, applying it to Judas.

options.text: It has no connection to any New Testament event.
options.note: The theme of betrayal by an intimate companion connects directly to the betrayal of Jesus by Judas.

options.text: It only applies to betrayal among modern political leaders.
options.note: The psalm's application is timeless and personal, not restricted to a particular modern political context.

options.text: It suggests that close friendship should always be avoided.
options.note: The psalm mourns a specific betrayal; it does not counsel against friendship or fellowship in general.

quiz.q: What is the psalm's ultimate resolution, despite ongoing treachery around David?

options.text: Settled trust in God, who hears, sustains, and will not let the righteous be shaken.
options.note: Verses 16-23 close the psalm in this confident trust, even while treachery continues.

options.text: Complete despair with no hope of resolution.
options.note: The psalm moves toward confident trust, not despair, by its conclusion.

options.text: A plan for David to personally punish his betrayer.
options.note: David entrusts judgment to God rather than planning personal punishment.

options.text: A resolve to permanently withdraw from all human relationships.
options.note: The psalm does not counsel total withdrawal from relationship, but trust in God amid painful ones.

questions: David honestly admits his longing to simply fly away from overwhelming pain. Is there a burden right now you long to escape entirely, and what would it look like to bring that honest longing to God rather than suppressing it?

David says an enemy's hostility he could endure, but betrayal by a close friend wounded him most deeply. Have you experienced betrayal from someone you trusted, and how does this psalm's honesty give you permission to grieve that specifically?
The psalm's turning point is a deliberate choice: cast your burden upon the LORD. What burden are you currently carrying that you need to consciously and deliberately transfer to God today?
David prays for God's justice on his betrayer rather than pursuing revenge himself. Where do you need to release a desire for personal payback and trust God's justice instead?

Jesus experienced betrayal by His own familiar friend, Judas, yet entrusted Himself fully to the Father. How does knowing Christ understands intimate betrayal firsthand change how you bring your own experience of betrayal to Him?

translationNotes.note: Sweet fellowship translates sod, a word for intimate, trusted counsel or companionship, intensifying the sense of betrayal since this was no casual acquaintance but a confidant.
Let them go down to Sheol alive echoes the judgment on Korah's rebellion in Numbers 16:30-33, invoking a similarly sudden and decisive act of divine judgment on treachery.
Cast your burden upon the LORD is quoted nearly verbatim in 1 Peter 5:7, showing the New Testament's direct dependence on this psalm's language and counsel.
